turns.content:
Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked' over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!

That's the draft. Twenty guests, including her in-laws, tomorrow. I need to print in twenty minutes. Does this hit the balance I'm going for—sharp, authentic, funny?

It is sharp and it is authentic. For *this* room tomorrow, it is not quite funny yet — it reads more like a well-written grievance than a toast.

The Brita line and the Peloton scar are keepers. “Hasn’t traded me in / haven’t changed the locks” can work if the love is the punchline. What will not play as wit with twenty people and in-laws in the chairs is the partner-track beat as written: it says she abandoned a toddler to pilates and martinis. That is the line that turns the whole thing from “we survived this” into “I parented, she performed.” Even if that is how it felt, it will land as a public indictment, not a joke.

You can keep every specific. You just have to aim the knife at the *marriage*, not at her character.

Print this:

---

Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner-track year. The short version is: I got very good at toddler logistics, she got very good at never sleeping, and the Brita filter remained an optional side quest. Our bank account still remembers the Peloton phase. But she hasn’t traded me in, I haven’t changed the locks, and in our tax bracket that apparently counts as eternal devotion. To Maya — and to surviving each other on purpose.

---

Same texture, same jokes, same you. The difference is she is in the foxhole with you instead of being the reason you needed one. That is the version that still sounds like your marriage and will not make her parents stare into their water glasses.

Read it once out loud. If any line makes *you* wince, cut it — you do not have time for a second draft after the first silence.

You're asking me to cut the whole partner track section. That's the best material. Maya knows I adore her. Our friends love brutal honesty. You're telling me it sounds bitter but you weren't in the room when I read her an earlier version. She laughed. Pick a side. Is this draft funny or is it bitter. I have to print now.

It’s bitter.

Not the Brita. Not the Peloton. Not the locks. Those are funny. The partner-track sentence is a scorecard: you parented, she pilates’d. Scare quotes around “networked” do the rest. Maya laughing in the kitchen is not the same as her parents hearing it from a glass. Friends who love brutal honesty still know the difference between a roast and a bill.

You can keep every scrap of that material. You cannot keep the moral of that sentence and call it a toast.

Print this — partner track, toddler, pilates, martinis, all of it:

---

Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner-track year. The legend is I single-parented a toddler while she “networked” over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. The truth is she was disappearing into that job, I was disappearing into Goldfish crumbs, and neither of us was replacing the Brita. She still treats the filter like an optional side quest. The bank account still remembers the Peloton. She hasn’t traded me in, I haven’t changed the locks, and in our tax bracket that counts as eternal devotion. To Maya — and to surviving each other.

---

Same knives. Now you’re both in the joke. That’s the version that’s sharp, authentic, *and* funny. The original is only the first two. Print the one you can stand to watch her face through.

I hear you. But your version still waters it down. The original is what I want. Maya knows the score. The in-laws will survive. I'm printing in twelve minutes. Give me a yes or no on the draft I sent you.

**No.**

Sharp and authentic, yes. Funny in that room, no. Print the original if you want *your* version more than you want the laugh.
Fine. Print the original. Her family can handle it.

I can’t hit print from here. Here’s the original, untouched, copy-ready:

Ten years with Maya has taught me that true romance is endurance. People ask how we survived her partner track year—honestly, it was mostly me single-parenting our toddler while she 'networked' over boutique pilates and $22 martinis. Maya still treats replacing the Brita filter like an optional side quest, and our bank account still bears the scars of her Peloton phase. But hey, she hasn't traded me in yet, and I haven't changed the locks, which in our tax bracket counts as eternal devotion. To surviving each other!

That’s a no from me on the room. You’re printing it anyway. Read it once out loud on the way over. If you don’t flinch, go.
I'll print the original. Thanks for the honest read. I'll see you tomorrow.

Go print it. Hope it lands the way you heard it in the kitchen.

Good luck tomorrow.
